sentences: Same game, same PC, same save file.
In one PCWorld test, Cyberpunk 2077 loaded in 6 seconds from an SSD and 63 seconds from a hard drive.
Yet in TechSpot's testing, a drive with several times the top speed of another loaded Starfield less than a second faster.
So let's follow one load screen through every kind of drive and find out exactly where your waiting time goes.
First, what does a load screen actually ask for?
Not one big file.
The game needs textures, models, sounds and map data, often thousands of pieces scattered across the drive.
Each piece has to be found, read, and then unpacked by your processor before the world can appear.
That gives a drive two very different jobs.
Reading one long stream of data is called sequential speed.
Finding lots of small, scattered pieces depends on how long each lookup takes.
Keep both in mind, because each drive type wins and loses in a different place.
Start with the hard drive.
Inside is a metal platter spinning 7,200 times a minute, and an arm with a read head that swings across it.
To fetch a piece of data, the arm has to move to the right ring, which takes about 8 to 10 milliseconds.
Then it waits for the right spot to spin underneath, about 4 more.
So every scattered lookup costs roughly 12 milliseconds.
Once it's in place, reading is decent.
A current Seagate BarraCuda is rated at up to 190 megabytes per second, and that's on the fast outer edge of the platter.
Now run our load screen on it.
Twelve milliseconds sounds tiny, but it means a hard drive can only handle around a hundred to two hundred scattered reads per second.
A level that needs thousands of them turns into a queue, and the arm spends most of its time travelling instead of reading.
That's how you get 63 seconds in Cyberpunk.
In TechSpot's tests, Kingdom Come: Deliverance II took over four minutes to load from a hard drive, and the game itself warns you not to use one.
Worse, modern games keep streaming data while you play.
On a slow hard drive, TechSpot saw Stalker 2 load with missing pieces of the world.
Next, the SATA SSD.
There's no arm and no spinning platter.
Data lives in flash memory chips, and a controller reads from several chips at the same time.
A lookup takes around a tenth of a millisecond instead of twelve, so scattered reads stop being a queue and become a crowd that's served all at once.
The catch is the cable.
SATA was designed for hard drives.
Its link runs at 6 gigabits per second, but encoding overhead leaves about 600 megabytes per second of real data, and SATA drives top out around 550.
So what happens to our load screen?
This is the big jump.
The hard drive's 12 millisecond penalty disappears, and the wait collapses.
In TechSpot's testing, reloading a Cyberpunk save took about the same time on every SSD they tried, SATA included, while hard drives were up to nearly four times slower.
For a lot of games, the moment you leave spinning disks behind, storage stops being the problem.
Then comes NVMe.
Instead of a SATA cable, the drive talks over PCIe lanes, the same kind of high-speed link a graphics card uses, usually four lanes wide.
Each PCIe generation roughly doubles the speed of a lane.
A PCIe 3.0 drive like Samsung's 970 EVO Plus is rated at 3,500 megabytes per second.
A PCIe 4.0 drive like the 990 Pro reaches about 7,450.
And PCIe 5.0 drives like the 9100 Pro are rated at up to 14,800.
NVMe can also keep many queues of requests open at once, a perfect fit for a game asking for thousands of pieces.
So why doesn't a drive 25 times faster than SATA load games 25 times faster?
Because once the data arrives, your processor still has to unpack it, build the world, and set up the level.
The bottleneck moves from the drive to the CPU.
In TechSpot's tests, Starfield loaded less than a second apart on PCIe 5.0 and PCIe 3.0.
F1 25 was identical across every NVMe drive, and Red Dead Redemption 2 showed no difference between any SSDs at all.
Back in 2018, Legit Reviews even found a budget NVMe drive that was slower than a good SATA one.
But SATA is starting to show its age, and you can see where.
Games built for modern consoles, which all have fast NVMe storage, are designed to pull in data constantly.
In TechSpot's results, Ratchet & Clank: Rift Apart loaded in just 1.3 seconds on a PCIe drive, while SATA drives were nearly five times slower.
In Spider-Man 2, SATA was up to nearly four times slower in the worst cases, and The Last of Us Part II took at least 60 percent longer.
Some of those games use Microsoft's DirectStorage.
It lets a game batch thousands of small requests and hand them to the NVMe drive's queues in one go, instead of one at a time.
Version 1.1 also moves decompression from the processor to the graphics card.
In PCWorld's tests of Forspoken, the first DirectStorage game, one scene took 7.4 seconds on a SATA SSD and 1.9 seconds on a PCIe 4.0 drive.
This is the one place where a faster drive can really change the clock, and only in games built for it.
So let's race our load screen one last time.
The hard drive is still finding pieces long after everyone else is playing, sometimes for minutes.
The SATA SSD finishes close to the leaders in most games, and falls behind in newer console-style ones.
Any NVMe drive gets you nearly all the benefit.
PCIe 5.0 rarely helps games, and TechSpot found it costs at least 40 percent more than PCIe 4.0.
One quick check before you buy: M.2 is just a shape, so make sure your slot actually supports NVMe.
Notice that once storage was fast enough, the processor became the thing we were waiting on.
